one_liner: Rust CRDT library compiled to WebAssembly; replays a real 260k-op editing trace about 1.85x faster than Yjs 13.6.
what_it_does: Loro is a CRDT framework for local-first and collaborative apps: a LoroDoc holds text, rich text, lists, movable lists, maps and movable trees that merge concurrent edits from peers, with time travel and Git-like version history. JavaScript uses the loro-crdt npm package (wasm-bindgen output for nodejs, bundler, browser, web and base64 targets); Rust uses the loro crate and Swift and other languages use loro-ffi. The API (getText/getList/getMap, export({mode}), import, commit) and the binary update and snapshot formats are its own, so it replaces Yjs rather than dropping in for it.
how_it_is_fast: The core is Rust compiled to wasm32: the text CRDT is Fugue, merging adapts the Event Graph Walker (Eg-walker) from diamond-types so concurrent ranges are replayed instead of keeping per-character CRDT metadata live, and operations are run-length encoded and held in an in-tree generic B-tree. Encoding is columnar (serde_columnar, after Automerge), and the snapshot format stores the operation log plus the encoded in-memory state, so loading skips replay; that is why B4 parseTime is 13 ms against Yjs's 39 ms while encodeTime and document size go the other way.
when_to_use: Long single-writer editing histories applied op by op: the B4 trace (259,778 single-character inserts and deletes) ran in 3,089 ms vs Yjs 5,714 ms on an i5-8400 with Node 20.5.0.
Apps that reload documents from a stored snapshot often and care about load time (B4 parseTime 13 ms vs 39 ms; B4x100 parseTime 1,304 ms vs 2,622 ms).
Data models beyond text, list and map: movable trees and lists, rich text, time travel and version control are built in.
Stacks that share one CRDT core across Rust, JavaScript/WebAssembly and Swift.
when_not_to_use: Tight bundle budgets: 1,052,250 bytes (399,276 gzipped) for loro 0.10.1 vs 69,124 (20,100) for Yjs, and 2,919,363 bytes for 1.0.0-beta.2 in Loro's own fork of the benchmark.
Workloads dominated by concurrent conflicting edits or frequent full encodes: Yjs is faster on B2.2-B2.4, B3.3 and B3.4, and B4x100 encodeTime is 14,429 ms vs 365 ms.
Bandwidth-sensitive per-keystroke sync: average update size is 109 bytes vs 27 for Yjs on B1.1.
Existing Yjs deployments: different API and wire format, so moving over means migrating documents and code.

Very large documents in the browser: wasm32 caps memory at 4 GiB, and issue #1092 (loro-crdt 1.15.1) showed container-by-container reads retaining about 4 KB per container until a trap, fixed by PR #1093 on 2026-09-04.

integration.form: module (npm loro-crdt, wasm plus JS bindings); crate (loro) for Rust
integration.dependencies: none at runtime for the npm package (self-contained wasm); the Rust crate pulls serde_columnar, rustc-hash, smallvec, xxhash-rust and other crates.io dependencies
integration.min_toolchain: Rust stable (rust-toolchain file; no rust-version declared); any JS runtime with WebAssembly (Node, browsers, Deno and Bun are in the package test script)
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host plus native Rust targets and Swift; other languages via loro-ffi
integration.thread_safety: Rust LoroDoc is Send but not built for shared concurrent use: internal try_lock().unwrap() panics on contention and the maintainer says to add an outer lock (issue #685, lock-hierarchy check added in PR #688); JS use is single-threaded

gotchas: Harness flaw in the source benchmark: in B1-B3 of dmonad/crdt-benchmarks the parseTime timer wraps getMemUsed() and logMemoryUsed(), each of which calls global.gc() (the suite runs node --expose-gc), so those rows include two forced full GCs whose cost grows with the JS heap; wasm libraries keep document state in linear memory that V8 does not trace, which likely biases B1-B3 parseTime against pure-JS Yjs (B1.2's 6 KB document takes 27-34 ms to parse in Yjs, ywasm and Loro alike, consistent with a GC-dominated floor). B4 parseTime is timed outside the GC calls, but every figure is a single perf.now() run rounded to milliseconds, and memUsed ignores wasm memory, so Loro's 0 B rows mean nothing.

The table is stale: it measured loro-crdt 0.10.1 (the harness pins ^0.10.1 and calls the pre-1.0 Loro, exportSnapshot and exportFrom APIs). Loro's own fork (zxch3n/crdt-benchmarks, MacBook Pro M1, loro 1.0.0-beta.2 vs Yjs 13.6.15 with gc disabled) shows B4 at 2,271 vs 2,616 ms, only about 1.15x (derived from page data), and says the 1.0 encoding is slower than the pre-1.0 one; the current release is 1.16.4.

Loro keeps the full operation history: in dmonad's table B3.3 (overwriting map string values) gives a 7,798,572-byte document vs 38,357 for Yjs, which garbage-collects overwritten values; shallow snapshots are the documented way to trim history.

Open data-loss bugs remain around LoroTree and undo/redo (#1055 undo after import deletes a pre-existing node ID; #938 redo loses text when a tree node is recreated), and #1117 reports a stack overflow in fork_at/checkout after concurrent tree moves.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Loro over ywasm (y-crdt) when long editing traces or snapshot loading dominate (B4 3,089 ms vs 28,675 ms) or you need movable trees, rich text or history, and over Automerge 2.x when load time matters (B4 parseTime 13 ms vs 1,805 ms) and you accept larger documents (258,228 vs 129,116 bytes). For text-only editing, compare diamond-types, the Eg-walker reference implementation whose algorithm Loro adapts.
verified_claims_summary: In dmonad/crdt-benchmarks, the suite maintained by the Yjs author, on an Intel i5-8400 with Node 20.5.0, the prebuilt loro-crdt 0.10.1 wasm package replayed the 259,778-op real-world editing trace in 3,089 ms vs 5,714 ms for Yjs 13.6.11 (1.85x), the 100x replay in 309,689 vs 608,908 ms (2.0x), and parsed its snapshot in 13 vs 39 ms. Yjs won encode time, document size, bundle size and most concurrent-conflict workloads, and all numbers come from single runs of a 2024 table.
status_note: Actively maintained (loro-crdt 1.16.4, 2,226 commits, 6.2k stars, MIT), but the independent numbers cover only the 0.10.1 release, so re-run the suite on 1.x before relying on the B4 margin.
